newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Retailers ringing up gains on Brussels bourse.
newsitem.headline: Retailers ringing up gains on Brussels bourse.

text.p: Shares in Belgium's three top retailers led the Brussels bourse higher on Wednesday, rising on a collection of reasons including expansion, restructuring, the prospect of positive results and a spin-off, dealers said.

Colruyt put on the most, gaining a solid 2.82 percent to 17,300 francs and outperforming the Bel-20 index which was up 0.76 percent at 2,373 points by 1245 GMT. GIB gained 20 francs at 1,730 and Delhaize was up 20 at 1,900.
Colruyt is due to announce 1996/1997 full year results after Thursday's bourse close.

Dealers said expectations for Colruyt results were positive. The consensus forecast as quoted on Reuters Equities 3000 is for earnings per share to rise to 654.50 francs in the year to March 1997 and to 723 francs in the year to March 1998.
Pre-tax EPS was 518 francs in the year to March 1996.
First-half 1996/97 consolidated net profit rose by 11.6 percent to 1.105 billion francs, Colruyt said in January.

One trader said most of the expected increase in earnings had already been discounted and that the share was still being bought on expectations the company stood to gain from the planned split-up of its Dolmen computer unit.
He cited market speculation that part of the unit might be sold off, or merged, or floated on the bourse.
Referring to recent listings in the computer sector he said, "Colruyt should do quite well out of that."
Shares in Real Software listed earlier this month at 1,500 francs each, were at 2,250 francs on Wednesday. Systemat was at 1,500 francs, up from its 1,175 franc launch price set in March.
The trader said Colruyt was also benefiting from a recent positive write-up in a major international newspaper.

Dealers said players liked GIB for its efforts at restructuring, notably by bringing various store names under the group umbrella with the goal of raising sales at its franchise partners by 20 percent over the two to three years.
"It's good for the image, it will give GIB more and centralised purchasing power and boost margins," a trader said.

GIB has also gained from talk that its search for a partner for some of its businesses, particularly its DIY outlets, might come to fruition and that its largest shareholder, holding company Cobepa, might part with its GIB shares.
Delhaize was in the spotlight after the company announced plans earlier this week to venture into the Far East.
It said on Monday a Thai supermarket chain joint venture aimed to have three stores in the first year, 10 in the second year and over 100 stores in five years' time.
On Tuesday it said it signed a long-term cooperation deal to develop a chain in Indonesia, expecting 50 "Super Indo" stores to be opened in five years' time.
